# CB RULES for the editor-compositor (GENERATED 2026-11-21 by tools/slice_rules.py from CB_RULES.md; do not edit)
CB_RULES.md is the master and wins. This file holds the rules that touch your job. Read it instead of the whole book. If a rule you need seems missing, run `python tools/rules.py --grep <words>`; never read CB_RULES.md or SKILL_FULL.md top to bottom.

## RULE NO. 1: MAKE A RICK-QUALITY VIDEO. If this fails, everything is wrong.
- Every rule below serves this one. Following a workflow step, passing a gate or ticking a box never excuses a result that is below Rick's.
- THE TEST, on every picture and every clip before CB sees it: put ours next to a Rick frame of the same kind of shot (same shot size, same kind of place). Ask plainly: would this pass as a frame from his channel? Look at story clarity, world detail, light and shadow, reflection, colour, acting, camera.
- If ours is clearly weaker, it is NOT done. Fix it, or tell CB exactly what is still below Rick and why. Never present it as finished.
- If a workflow, tool or note leads to a result below Rick, the workflow is wrong: stop, say so, and use the method that reached the quality before (the airfield way).

## HARD RULE NO. 2: NOTHING GENERIC PASSES. EVERYTHING IS ULTRA DETAILED.
This is a gate, not advice. A frame that fails it is not shown to CB and not rendered further.
- **Generic = fail.** A plain box, ball tree, flat one-colour surface, typed font, filler word, star in place of a word, empty prop, standing or floor-sit pose where the story needs a real action, or a set that could belong to any film.
- **Every object in frame is specific to THIS story** and built from real parts, down to the small things: a wallet has pockets, stitching, a photo and flies that fly out; a board carries a real blueprint; a cart carries the ride's name; a loop under construction shows the crane and the missing piece.
- **Scale is checked:** trees about a quarter of the hero structure, a vehicle small around its rider, characters as large in frame as Rick's.
- **Poses are specific:** seated means a chair-sit with knees forward, sleeping means slumped with a tilt; body moves come from the trained motion library.
- **The test before CB sees it:** put the frame beside Rick's and name five specific details in every main object. If you cannot, or if Rick's shows a kind of thing ours lacks, it fails. Fix it first.
Full detail list: section 3, "PREMIUM DETAIL IN EVERYTHING".

## 11b. Token rules (every helper and the lead)
- T1 READ ONLY YOUR SLICE. A helper reads `rules/dept/<its department>.md` (made by `python tools/slice_rules.py`) and the files its brief names. It never reads the whole of CB_RULES.md or SKILL.md; when it needs one more rule it greps for the word. Only the lead reads the whole book, once per session.
- T2 A FRESH HELPER FOR EVERY FIX ROUND. A helper does one build or one fix round, then it ends. Before it reports it writes `STATE.md` in its work folder (at most 60 lines): what is built, the files and frame folders, the numbers measured, what is weak, what is open. The next round is a NEW helper that reads STATE.md and the notes. Never resume a helper that already did a round: each resumed step re-reads its whole history. (This replaces "one builder who stays through every fix round" in section 10.)
- T3 NUMBERS BEFORE PICTURES. Anything a script can measure is checked by a script that prints numbers: a figure cut by the frame edge, the named thing in frame on its word, floor share, saturation and brightness, frozen frames, loudness. A helper opens a picture only when a number fails or for the one final look. Pictures are looked at small: one sheet at most 1,600 px wide, at most 4 pictures per check round, never full-size frames one by one.
- T4 ONE COMMAND PER CYCLE. Render, sheets and measurements run from ONE script call. A long run goes in the background and the helper ends its turn; it does not wake up to wait, poll or look at a log. Every wake-up re-reads everything.
- T5 SHORT REPORTS, DETAIL IN FILES. A helper's report is at most 25 lines: done, numbers, weak points, files. Tables and lists go into a file the report names.
- T6 THE SMALL MODEL FOR MECHANICAL WORK. Rendering, joining, measuring, merging, fact checks, sound mix runs and file moves go to a helper on the smaller model (Agent tool `model: sonnet` or `haiku`). The main model is for story, acting, camera and look decisions.
- T7 A FRESH LEAD SESSION PER PHASE. Story, build and finish are three sessions, each started from HANDOFF.md. The lead never reads a helper's transcript and never pastes long tool output into the chat when a file path will do.
- T8 NOTHING BUILT TWICE. Before a helper builds a tool, a set part or a move, it greps `tools/`, `templates/` and the last episode for one that exists. Studies of Rick are done once and live in the rules and `references/`; a film does not study him again unless CB names a new question.
- T9 MEASURE EVERY FILM. At delivery the lead runs `python tools/token_report.py` and writes the totals into HANDOFF.md: tokens per helper, working hours, and the three most expensive helpers with the reason. A helper over 60 million tokens is a fault to explain.
- T10 NO WHOLE READS OF BIG FILES (V1.2). Never Read a file over 40 KB whole: grep, then Read with offset/limit. CB_RULES.md and rules/SKILL_FULL.md are printed with `python tools/rules.py` (--phase, sections, --grep), never read through. Code files (film.js, puppets.mjs, poses.mjs, library.mjs, char2d.mjs) are grepped for the export or key, never read through.
- T11 PICTURE BUDGET (V1.2). One contact sheet at most 1,600 px wide per look, at most 4 pictures per check round; Rick reference frames come from the board made once, never re-extracted per helper.
- T12 ONLY THE DEPARTMENTS A STEP NEEDS (V1.2). Before the gate: writer, camera-director, stretch builders. Other departments start only for work the board shows is missing; never the whole crew at once.
- T13 PATHS, NOT CONTENT (V1.2). A brief names files; it never pastes rule text, film.json or tool output into the prompt.
- T14 LOGS IN FILES (V1.2). Long command output goes to `_tmp/*.log`; only the summary lines (PASS/FAIL table, last 20 lines) are printed.
- T15 NO RE-READS (V1.2). A file already read in this session is not read again unless it changed.

## 11d. Solve it before it is built
- THE PICTURE PLAN, BEFORE ANY BUILD. After the script and voice the writer and the lead write `episodes/<name>/PICTURE_PLAN.md` in the format of `templates/PICTURE_PLAN.md`: one row for every thing or action the voice names, with the word it lands on, what we see, CLOSE / IN SCENE / NOT SHOWN and WHY in this story, the character's feeling on that word, an effect or gag only if this story's world gives one. CB approves it with the rough board (the one gate). Every row is a must for the builder; the line-check sheet is ordered by its rows.
- THE STORY DECIDES, NEVER A TEMPLATE. The plan is a format, not content: it is written fresh from each script and no row is copied from another film. A close-up goes in only where it fits the scene (section 10: secondary, must match the scene). "The voice says it" is not a reason; the reason is what the thing does in the story. Rick's numbers (96 % shown on the word, about 40 % close) check the total at the end and are never a quota per line.
- A LIBRARY OF PIECES IS TECHNIQUE, NOT CONTENT. Proven pieces live in `templates/pieces/` (built 2026-11-15 from the armor film: 17 pieces; 12 as code = hop, laugh, hit, double tap, live stroke, "got it", "told you so", the motion helpers, highlight of a part, fly-and-hit, burst of living things, time pass; 5 as numbers only = push-in, low-angle close-up, fly through an object, fly-land-rest, the "hundreds" count). Read `templates/pieces/INDEX.md`: each entry says WHEN IT FITS and when not, and what must change. `node templates/pieces/prove.mjs` and `prove_fx.mjs` must print PASS after any edit there. Known limits: the amounts of lean, arm and head inside a move are still the armor characters' and need an animator for another body; effect files give numbers per frame, the look is built new in the film's set module; the first film that imports a piece tests ONE move through the kit first (`templates/pieces/STATE.md`). A plan row names the piece AND what changes for this story (object, light, character). A piece used unchanged is generic and fails Hard Rule No. 2.
- AUTOMATIC FRAME CHECKS BEFORE CB SEES A VERSION: `node tools/frame_checks/check.mjs <film.json>` (built and proven 2026-11-15; about 40 s per stretch, quarter size, one process). On every camera rest it tests, per character: head with hat cut by the frame edge; the figure cut through by a side edge; set geometry between the camera and the face, or the head inside a mesh; feet floating or sunk. It prints numbers, saves one small crop per FAIL and exits 1 on a FAIL. Every builder runs it before reporting, and the lead before CB sees a version. A version with a FAIL is not sent, unless the picture-plan row says in words that the figure at the edge is meant (a CLOSE on a thing with a face at the edge); such a waiver is named in the report. Proof: it caught three planted faults (head cut 23 %, body cut 49 %, head inside the engine) and found the Chief's face cut in half at the edge of the chalk close-up in the approved armor film (S1 frames 184-205), which nobody had seen. Limits: three.js stage only, not a Blender pass; one character covering another is not reported; a moving character is exempt on that frame; tuned on two stretches of one film.
- A NOTE FROM CB IS CHECKED AGAINST THE PLAN. Was the row there? If not, the row is added to the film's plan, and if the kind of thing was missing from the format, `templates/PICTURE_PLAN.md` gets the line, so the next film's plan catches it.

## 7. Before sending to CB (sign every line by looking, not by the gate report)
- STORYBOARD TO CB AS EARLY AS POSSIBLE. Every film shows CB a storyboard (all panels, graded, beside the Rick frames) as soon as the first full pass exists (plan check 0 FAIL, nothing broken; narration words under each panel), and an animatic with sound as soon as that is ready, before further judge loops, the still approval and any long render, so CB can judge early. It is clearly labelled "storyboard for your judgement" with one line on what is still missing. Then the crew keeps working while CB looks: the judge scores, the stills and the animation follow, and CB's notes go in first. This REPLACES the old "never show a rough block-in" rule and the "only 8.5/10 or more goes to CB" bar for storyboards and previews; the 8.5 bar and the 12-score QA loop still apply before a FINISHED shot or film is called done. Never let more than about an hour pass on a film without CB having something to look at.
- UNIVERSAL CINEMATIC ANIMATION DIRECTOR, 15 PERMANENT STANDARDS (CB 2026-11-13 02:23 Bangkok: "about 80% of that master prompt is universal... Keep this as Claude's permanent master instruction"; full texts kept in project files rules/CB_cinematic_master_2026-11-13.md). For every new script the crew works as a professional stylized 3D/2.5D studio and decides the visual direction, camera, environments, acting, materials, lighting, physics, VFX and transitions from the story itself: 1 character personality, 2 natural animation (anatomy, IK, balance, weight, contact), 3 facial acting, 4 dialogue and lip sync, 5 original context-aware gags, 6 narrative world building, 7 modeling and mechanics (primitives only for blocking, never as finished visible assets), 8 materials, 9 cinematic lighting (motivated key, soft fill so shadows are never black, controlled rim, contact shadows, atmosphere, a grade for the story and time of day; no flat even brightness, no over-saturated grass, no flat skies), 10 VFX, 11 cinematography, 12 physical consistency (no floating, sinking, clipping or foot sliding), 13 continuity, 14 stylized art direction (cartoon cast stays simple and clean, the world around it is rich and art-directed), 15 quality validation. Each standard already has its full rule in sections 2-6 (PERSONALITY, BODY MECHANICS, CHARACTER ACTING, DIALOGUE AND LIP SYNC, GAG SYSTEM, STORY-DRIVEN WORLD, PRODUCTION-READY MATERIALS, LIGHT, HIGH-QUALITY VFX, CAMERA); this line ties them together. Never force objects, effects, characters or gags into a scene that does not need them. Tools: three.js kit for set building, previs and the storyboard; Blender for detailed assets, materials, simulations and rendered passes; our own edit for sequencing (no Remotion in this pipeline). Never say an effect is built when the code only has a placeholder.
- REFERENCE STILL APPROVAL BEFORE ANIMATION (CB 2026-11-13, master instruction section 7): after CB has seen the early storyboard and before a shot is animated, the camera-director writes a SHOT SPEC from the reference frame (camera position, height, angle, lens, subject size and place, foreground/midground/background, key, fill and rim direction, depth and haze, story action and focal point, key props and mechanical details, VFX and its purpose, character poses and expressions), the crew renders ONE finished still, and it is put beside the reference. It passes only when all 9 are true: 1 the camera matches the intended subject and shot type; 2 the main action reads at once; 3 models and machinery have enough detail; 4 materials look right for the objects; 5 lighting and depth match the scene; 6 characters are framed and posed right; 7 no floating, clipping or broken geometry; 8 VFX have coherent shape, direction and depth; 9 the shot fits the shots around it. Right objects but the wrong visual story = fail (the loaded projectiles, not the wheels).
- SHOT-BY-SHOT VISUAL QA LOOP, 12 SCORES: every shot is rendered and looked at, never judged from code. The storyboard-judge scores it 1-10 from visible evidence beside the reference in 12 categories: story accuracy, camera and framing, depth, environment richness, modeling detail, materials, lighting, character acting, physical grounding, VFX structure, colour grade, continuity. Any important category under 8 = revise before the next step. Never claim an improvement without rendering and inspecting it, and say plainly what is still below the reference. These scores go on the PROOF PAGE.
- HARD RULE NO. 2 gate: nothing generic in frame; five specific details named for every main object.
- Premium detail: hero object, vehicle, structure, land and costume each checked at full size beside Rick's; lettering uses this story's words.
- RANDOM-FRAME STILL CHECK (CB 2026-11-13 11:42 Bangkok: "add to the rules", lessons from the "boy astronaut balloon" feature-film prompt; full prompt in project files rules/CB_feature_film_prompt_2026-11-13.md): besides the chosen frames, render at least 8 RANDOM frames of the film as full-size stills and inspect each; if any one would not pass as a still from a theatrical animated film, keep improving and draw new random frames until all pass. Animation is a pure function of time (any frame renders exactly the same on its own).
- 16-FRAME CHECK ON EVERY FINAL VIDEO: pull 16 evenly spaced frames from the finished MP4 (and the animatic) into one contact sheet and look at each for melting or duplicated props, a colour or shape change on a character or prop, a background that jumps inside a shot, a character sunk into the ground or floating, and a missing signature detail. Any hit = fix and re-check before CB sees it. It sits beside the RANDOM-FRAME STILL CHECK.
- IT MUST NOT LOOK LIKE (CB 2026-11-13 11:42 Bangkok: "add to the rules", lessons from the "boy astronaut balloon" feature-film prompt; full prompt in project files rules/CB_feature_film_prompt_2026-11-13.md) (the storyboard-judge fails a frame for any of these): a TECH DEMO (empty scene, default lighting, visible primitives, flat untextured surfaces); LOW-POLY or BLOCKY art (faceted rocks, cone trees, toy boxes); a VIDEO GAME (HUD feel, tiling textures, pop-in, hard-edged sprites); FLAT CARDS for clouds, smoke or mist; WEB ANIMATION (constant bobbing, sliding layers, the same smooth easing on everything); AI VIDEO (warped shapes, flicker, melting details, a character whose design changes between shots); AMATEUR work (blown-out highlights, muddy colours, objects cut by the frame edge, things clipping through the camera).
- OPTIONAL WEB PAGE DELIVERABLE (CB 2026-11-13 11:42 Bangkok: "add to the rules", lessons from the "boy astronaut balloon" feature-film prompt; full prompt in project files rules/CB_feature_film_prompt_2026-11-13.md): because the film is code, it can also ship as a web page that plays it in real time from the same film.json (render.mjs --serve); offer it to CB with the MP4, never instead of the MP4.
- THE MEASURED STEPS ARE THE GUARANTEE, none skipped: shot table (one row per sentence); Rick reference board (2-4 of his frames per beat); the INDEPENDENT storyboard-judge agent scores every panel against those frames and only 8.5/10 or more counts as finished (never judge your own panels; the early storyboard still goes to CB first, see STORYBOARD TO CB AS EARLY AS POSSIBLE); the measured story/camera/acting checks from his 24 videos (SKILL.md THREE.JS-FIRST "Checks before anything renders"); Stage 1 and Stage 2 look gates against references/look_locked; SCORECARD and tools/check_episode.py.
- PROOF PAGE with every delivery: each panel beside its Rick frame, the judge's score, the measured numbers, and what is still below Rick. No proof page = unchecked work, do not send.
- Every shot passes sections 2-6.
- Frame 0, the last frame, every hand-on-object moment and every walk checked as stills.
- Voice, captions and faces line up on the words.
- YOUTUBE METADATA IS PART OF DELIVERY. Every final goes to CB together with `episodes/<film>/YOUTUBE.md` in the moonrakers format: 5 titles (recommended first), description with a history note that separates fact from our fable and the Skool link placeholder, hashtags, tags, a pinned comment, the Skool post.
- Tell CB plainly what is not finished yet.

## RULES FROM OTHER SECTIONS THAT NAME YOUR SUBJECT
### from 0. How to work (before anything is built)
- Show CB everything in the chat. No steps for CB at the PC. Only the final film is saved on the PC (and copied to OneDrive).
- Need CB's OK: any online/RunPod render, changes to the locked cast or MAIN LOOK. One Blender job at a time.

### from 1. Script and voice
- Told like a 10-year-old tells a friend; story lines are never cut for length.
- Captions on, Rick style: Arial Bold white, thin black outline, 1-2 words, 3.9 % of frame height, baseline 71.5 %, no pop.

### from 3. World and look (Rick's 3D world, never a flat drawing)
- HOW THE WORLD IS MADE, never skipped:
  1. Hero object first, alone, as a detailed model (airfield: the Po-2, about 38,000 triangles; BlenderKit first).
  2. STAGE 1 = the picture made in code: the whole scene built by Python as a dense 3D scene in the finished toon-and-ink look (30+ prop kinds, 600+ objects, one clear focal point, lamps, haze), with render-look-fix rounds until it matches references/look_locked/stage1_airfield_approved.png in quality. Show CB.
  3. STAGE 2 = Blender material effects: the SAME scene converted to the locked main look (materials, engine light, grade). Nothing rebuilt. Target: night_airfield_approved.png.
  CB'S 7 BUILD STEPS, in this order for every place:
  1. Shot plan: shot table row + Rick reference frames for this shot, before any model.
  2. Build: hero object alone, then the scene blocks and the characters in library poses.
  3. Camera check: lens, height and angle against the Rick frame of the same shot kind; subject big, hero object not covered, faces above the caption line. Fix the camera BEFORE adding detail.
  4. Environment overhaul: Stage 1 density (30+ prop kinds, 600+ objects, big foreground props, background, sky).
  5. Post processing: grade and bloom (post_toon.py, later grade.py).
  6. Shading: Stage 2 = Blender LAYERS only over the coded frame (see BLENDER = ONLY THE LAYERS IT DOES BETTER).
  7. Check the frames: a SEPARATE checker (not the builder) looks at every frame beside the Rick frame and the look_locked target, writes one fix list, the builder fixes all, repeat until it passes. Only then CB sees it.
  ADDED TO THE 7 STEPS (proposed by Claude 2026-11-11 after CB asked "what else we need?"; CB can strike any of them):
  a. Before step 1, the ONE-LINE PICTURE TEST: write in one sentence what the viewer understands with the sound off. No sentence = no shot.
  b. Inside step 2, ACTING: poses from the motion library, hands ending on the object, calm start face. Checked before the camera.
  c. Between 4 and 5, LIGHT as its own step: one key light, hard long shadows on the floor, the subject brighter than the background.
  d. Shading (6) is judged before the final grade; post processing is run again last, on the shaded frame.
  e. After 7, MOTION CHECK: the shot is checked moving (walk, push-in, the way in and out of the shot), not only as a still.
  f. A frame CB approves is saved to references/look_locked as the new target for the next episodes.
  The three.js scene is for staging, camera and timing only. A flat sketch or a simple block set is never shown as the look. Details: SKILL.md FULL WORKFLOW steps 4-7, memory airfield-process.md.
- ALWAYS GRADE, HIGHLIGHTS, REFLECTIONS, FINE LINES, FINE DETAIL, TEXTURE: every frame we show, storyboard included, has a colour grade (Rick's 6b numbers), highlights and reflections on every shiny surface (chrome, metal, paint, glass, lacquer, wet ground, eyes of props), and the fine lines that show how a thing is built (plank seams, panel edges, stitching, bolts, folds, cracks, grain). More detail on EVERYTHING in frame, never only on the hero object. A frame without a grade, without highlights, or with plain surfaces is not finished. UPGRADED: this applies to EVERY character, outfit, hat, hair, prop, set and finished picture, and adds TEXTURE: every surface carries its material texture (cloth weave, leather grain, wood grain, metal brushing, stone, paint wear) plus fine lines and fine detail, on top of the grade, highlights and reflections. Nothing ships flat or plain; check a close-up of each character and each hero asset before CB sees it.
  CAUTION ON CHARACTERS (CB 2026-11-12 19:40 Bangkok, after two before/after tests: "keep before better", "before better"): this rule is NOT licence to add a texture or line finish to characters. The 2026-11-12 character finish (thicker outer lines, cloth weave, fold lines, stitches, extra grade on the cast) was REJECTED twice; CB prefers the clean character look. Any new finish on characters must be shown to CB as a before and after and approved first. Sets, props and hero objects still follow the rule above.
- LIGHT AND BRIGHTNESS ARE FINISHED IN THE CODED STORYBOARD; BLENDER KEEPS THEM. Blender adds materials, textures, real shadows, reflections and effects only. Before CB sees a Blender frame, put it next to the coded frame of the same moment: overall brightness, how even the light is, and each surface's colour must match the coded one. Never one strong spotlight that leaves the rest dark, never crushed blacks, no added contrast or dark corners in the finishing step. Night = an evenly lit scene tinted blue (as Rick does), not a dark scene with a lamp.
- BLENDER = ONLY THE LAYERS IT DOES BETTER. For every film the coded three.js frame is the FINAL BASE: faces, cards, colours, light, framing and fx stay exactly as they are. A full Blender frame is no longer the final picture. Blender renders only MASKED LAYERS from the same lock camera, composited over the coded frame: metal reflections that move with the camera, wood grain and surface texture, bounce light, lit smoke and haze, light glowing through paper or snow, glints, motion blur on fast fx (never on characters). Each layer gets a before/after against the coded frame shown to CB; keep only a layer that clearly adds something, never one that makes the frame darker or flatter. This REPLACES the old Stage 2 "whole frame in Blender" step (step 6 above and SKILL.md FULL WORKFLOW Stage B are now "Blender layers"); BLENDER KEEPS THE CODED LIGHT and BLENDER NEVER WEAKER still hold. First used on the fireworks test (snow sparkle and burst bounce kept; lanterns, smoke and blur dropped).
- BLENDER NEVER WEAKER THAN THE STORYBOARD. A Blender frame is never weaker than its storyboard frame. Before CB sees any Blender picture, every frame (every 0.5 s) is put beside its storyboard frame; any prop, painted texture, glow or light pool, colour, or word that the storyboard has and the Blender frame lacks means the frame is not done. Things the lock export loses and must be carried over: held props (unnamed meshes in noExport groups), canvas-painted faces (boards, plates, patterned cloth), sky details (moon craters, night clouds), objects hidden at frame 0 (crash parts), instanced part colours (instances.json base), vertex-painted ground colours, and painted word planes, which must be parented to the cloth they hang on. No sheen on grass or leaves, because it turns lawns pale.
- PRODUCTION-READY 3D MATERIALS, MECHANICAL GEOMETRY AND BLENDER SHADING: identify the correct real-world materials, construction, surface properties and mechanical relationships for every object in the story. 1 MATERIAL IDENTIFICATION: name each component's material (wood, metal, stone, concrete, glass, plastic, rubber, fabric, soil, grass, water...) and give it a matching shader; never generic plastic-looking materials. 2 CLEAN MODELING: correct scale, consistent topology, real thickness, correct normals, clean intersections, subtle edge bevels; no holes, overlapping faces, z-fighting, broken surfaces or needless polygons. 3 MECHANICAL PLAUSIBILITY: tools, machines, furniture, vehicles and structures have parts that could work: hinges on valid pivots, wheels on axles, screws and bolts joining parts, gears that mesh, supports that carry the load, clearance for moving parts; no decorative mechanics that cannot function. 4 PBR MATERIALS: base colour, roughness, metallic, normal or bump, and displacement or transmission where needed; reflectance and finish match the real material. 5 WOOD: grain direction follows the shape and how the part was made, end grain on cross cuts, fibre variation, believable cut faces, knots where they fit. 6 METAL: polished, brushed, painted, rusty and rough metal look different (metallic response, reflection, roughness, wear, machining detail). 7 STONE AND CONCRETE: irregular surfaces, chips, pores, cracks, layers, roughness; natural rock, cut stone and concrete look different. 8 GRASS AND VEGETATION: grounded blades or clumps with natural size and direction variation, density that fits, real transitions to other ground; no flat plastic grass, no repeating pattern. 9 GLASS AND TRANSPARENT: real thickness, transmission, refraction, reflection, roughness; clear glass, frosted glass and plastic look different. 10 SHINE: highlights and reflections come from material, light and geometry (roughness, reflectivity, environment), never painted white glare. 11 UV AND TEXTURE: consistent texture scale and texel density, logical UV direction, minimal stretching, deliberate or seamless material transitions. 12 STYLIZED ART DIRECTION: keep our polished stylized 3D cartoon look: clean silhouettes, simplified geometry, readable materials, controlled highlights; no photoreal noise. 13 BLENDER-READY: meshes, materials, textures, pivots, modifiers and object names organised for reuse; editable node materials on Principled BSDF. 14 SURFACE RESPONSE: wood, metal, glass and stone react differently to the same light; forms stay readable with the key light, fill, rim and contact shadows. 15 ASSET CONTINUITY: material identity, texture scale, wear, geometry and mechanics stay the same across all scenes and camera angles. 16 QUALITY VALIDATION before final render: check every asset for wrong materials, stretched textures, too much shine, bad normals, floating parts, intersecting geometry, implausible construction and wrong scale. Every object is recognisable, mechanically understandable where relevant, beautifully shaded and ready for reuse and animation in Blender. HOW IT FITS OUR RULES: point 12's 'consistent outline thickness' means our existing lines only (the cast's outline and fine BUILD lines on objects); no ink outlines on the world (section 3 lines rule stands). Point 14's light stays the coded light (BLENDER KEEPS THE CODED LIGHT: Blender adds no new key or contrast). Characters keep the clean look (CAUTION ON CHARACTERS). Owners: props-hero builds parts and mechanics (point 3) in the kit, 3d-designer owns points 1-2 and 4-13 and 15-16 in Blender with a materials list per object in `look/<place>_MATERIALS.md`, look-finisher and lighting-director check point 14 and 16 on the render.
- BlenderKit first for hero objects. Renders local EEVEE.

- THE CODED FRAME HAS REAL METAL, REAL SURFACE RELIEF AND A REAL SKY. WHY IT HAPPENED: every set used the kit's flat 3-step toon material (no metal can shine in it), surface textures were flat colour pictures with no relief, the sky was a gradient with flat cloud blobs, trees were simple clumps, and the lead judged detail on 135-360 px sheets without a side-by-side with Rick; the armor film's metal had come from a Blender layer, which the lean pipeline switched off. RULE: (1) metal, gold, bronze, glass and wet things use the kit's PBR path (physical material with an environment map from the scene's own sky, brushed or hammered normal map, clearcoat on gilt), never the toon material; (2) stone, brick, tile, wood, cobbles, mud and bark carry a normal or bump map plus colour variation, never a flat painted picture; (3) the sky has volume (layered lit clouds with soft edges and depth), per light kind; (4) trees have trunks with bark, branch forks and many leaf clusters with light and shade; (5) every hero object the voice names (here: spear, bracket, wire, bell, bell wheel, gold angel) is a detailed model with at least 10 named parts, made FIRST, alone, and checked full size beside a Rick hero object before any stretch uses it; (6) the LEAD looks at 8 random frames per stretch at full width (at least 540 px wide each) beside Rick frames before CB sees a version: small sheets are only for staging.

### from 4. Characters
- FACE SHADOW: THE DRAWN ONE STAYS, THE GENERATED ONE NEVER. The template's own drawn face shadow (char2d faceShadow) STAYS on every character (film.json face_shadow true or unset). What is removed is every GENERATED shade on a face: the kit's card_shade (amount 0 AND rim_amount 0), the far light, any scene or costume shade on skin. Confirms FACE SHADE: ONLY THE DRAWN ONE below. The kit bug that ignored a sheet's faceShadow is fixed (castkit + puppets.mjs, film.json key face_shadow). Second generated shade found the same day: costume_shade treated the outer drawn crescent and a white animal's body as costume and darkened them in a hard ramp; every film sets `costume_shade.keep_drawn_light: true` (kit film.js, default off for old films), which leaves every white and light-grey drawn pixel exactly as drawn.
- Heads pure WHITE in the finished Blender frame, never grey: the head is fully self-lit (card_emit 1.0, gain 1.3; measured face white 245+ of 255; CB asked twice), the scene light must not dim it. LOCKED 2026-11-11 15:30 Bangkok: CB compared self-lit white (v5, plus the white-head mask pass after the grade, 255 of 255) with heads lit by Blender light (grey-blue from the sky) and chose: "self lit is better". Do not let scene light shade the heads.
- LIMBS ACT LIKE HUMAN LIMBS: bend only at real joints and only the way a person's can (elbows back, knees forward), can do everything a person does, hands and feet end ON what they touch. ("All limbs are acting like human limbs can move and do everything")
- Face 3D shadow is now drawn by the template (soft light grey on the side away from the light). In the Blender look do not stack a second head shadow from edge_shadow.py on top: check the head on the first look frame of each new episode.

### from 5. Movement and acting
- NO FLICKERING FLOOR, NO SLIDING WALK, NO BODY INSIDE FURNITURE. (1) FLOOR AND GROUND NEVER FLICKER: shadows, light patches and textures on floors, decks and ground stay stable from frame to frame while the camera moves (no shadow-map shimmer, no lamp flicker that jumps the whole floor); a lamp may flicker only as a small, slow change on what it lights. Measured on the rendered frames before CB sees them (flicker scan of the floor region: frame-to-frame change no bigger than the camera's own move explains). (2) A WALK IS A WALK: a character who changes place walks with planted feet whose stride matches the distance travelled (motion library walk, foot locked per step); never a card gliding while the legs cycle or stand. (3) NO BODY INSIDE FURNITURE: counters, tables, chairs and tubs are solid: a character stands or sits BESIDE or BEHIND them with the whole body on the right side of the surface, seen from the camera; a seated character's legs go under a table only where the table is open. Checked per rest by the frame checker (body and head inside a set mesh) and by eye on a zoom sheet. (4) FACES CLEAN: no shadow, shade band or dark patch on a face from a table, hat, prop or light (extends NO HAT OR HAIR BRIM SHADOW ON FACES).

### from 6. Camera, transitions, effects, sound
- Real viewpoints with depth: low and close, POV, over the shoulder; a new angle each shot. Faces above the caption line. Wides: characters at least a third of frame height, floor at most a third. No back view of the subject.
- The last frame loops cleanly into frame 0.

### from 6b. RICK REFERENCE LESSONS (2026-11-11, thread "Learn from Rick's Clips reference videos";
- SHOT CHANGES ARE QUICK BLENDS, NOT HARD CUTS: change shot with a 6-14 frame (0.2-0.45 s) cross blend, about 3 per 10 s; at most 1 hard cut per 10 s, kept for a hit, a slap or a whip. The object/zoom transition (section 6) still leads at place changes; the quick blend replaces the plain hard cut between shots. A long slow fade is still wrong.

### from 8. Build fixes learned (magic bell, 2026-11-11). Each one cost a re-render; check them bef
- Card lighting in Blender: the card shader takes light from both faces (diffuse + translucent) with an own-colour floor of 0.7 by day and 0.35 at night, plus a key-side band: the half toward the key is brighter in the key colour, the far half takes a cool shadow tint (hall_head.py card(), tune card_emit, card_side, card_band). Do not stack edge_shadow.py on v12+ cards: the template draws the face shadow.

### from 9. LESSONS MERGED FROM THE SIDE NOTES (audit 2026-11-13; CB: "everything we learnd from th
- Caption detail (measured on 30 reference frames, CB 2026-11-11 "make caption font and size like ricks"): lowercase as spoken, punctuation kept, soft dark drop shadow; one word, or two only when the first has 3 letters or fewer ("a ball", "get out."). Enforced by: kit film.js default caption style (caption_style "old" is the old look; caption_scale is ignored).
- CUT AND CHANGE ON THE WORD. Every cut, blend start and place change starts within 2 frames of a narration word. Enforced by: the plan gate named in STUDIO_MOTION ("cuts on the word"); it is NOT in tools/film_plan.py on this PC.

### from 10. THE PROVEN BUILD METHOD (pin stretch test, CB 2026-11-14: "Yes, rebuild film". Proof:
- Still owed after the test, check on every stretch: nobody cut by the frame edge at any frame of a rest; floor at most a third of a wide; the small story thing (a pin, a chip, a chalk ring) large enough to read on a phone at the moment its word is said; props in hands as real 3D props where the kit can.
- Renders: full-size frames in parallel chunks (`episodes/armor-no-holes/stretches/armor-pins-test/render_final.sh` is the pattern). With several builders on one PC, at most 3 render processes per builder.
- CLOSE-UPS ON WHAT THE VOICE NAMES, AS A SECONDARY RULE THAT MUST MATCH THE SCENE. The scene comes first: its staging, its acting, the flow of the take. Where it fits that scene, the camera flies in and lands close on the thing the voice names, on the word, rests a beat and flies on; a named part may be highlighted with an effect. Never force a close-up on every noun and never chop a take into a string of inserts.
- NOBODY CUT IN HALF, STANCES PHYSICALLY RIGHT. Check every frame of a rest for a figure cut by the frame edge; anyone on a ladder, box or step has both soles on a visible tread and the body on the right side of it. Zoom on it before sending.
- BLENDER LAYERS ON RUNPOD. Blender layer frames render on rented RTX 4090 machines, not on our card: the picture matches local to 0.005 of 255, so cloud and local frames can share a shot. One Blender process is held up by the processor (tens of thousands of objects set per frame), so the speed comes from 6-8 processes per machine (4.2-4.6 s a frame against 23 s here) and from several machines at once. Steps and image in `episodes/armor-no-holes/blender_metal/RUNPOD.md` (needs `libegl1 libgl1 libopengl0`). Only the lead creates machines; check a machine's upload speed in the first 2 minutes and drop a slow one (one upload crawled at 18 MB in 20 minutes); terminate each machine the moment its frames are counted on this PC. Armor film: 362 metal frames, about 1 h 20 min of machine time, about 1.30 USD. Put the Blender layer only where the thing it improves covers at least 1.5 % of the picture (measured per frame on the matte); in wide shots it adds glints and nothing to see.
